title: Great Depression begins
summary: The 1929 Wall Street Crash triggered a deflationary depression and waves of bank failures. Gold hoarding and convertibility pressure mounted as the public lost faith in banks.

title: Executive Order 6102 (Roosevelt gold program)
summary: Roosevelt suspended dollar-gold convertibility and ordered Americans to surrender most private gold at $20.67/oz, ending the domestic gold standard and enabling devaluation.

title: Gold Reserve Act revalues gold to $35
summary: The Gold Reserve Act of 1934 transferred gold to the Treasury and revalued it from $20.67 to $35/oz, a ~41% dollar devaluation that boosted reserves and reflated prices.

title: Bretton Woods system established
summary: The 1944 Bretton Woods conference created a USD-centered monetary order with the dollar convertible to gold at $35/oz and other currencies pegged to the dollar.

title: London Gold Pool defends the $35 price
summary: Major central banks pooled reserves to hold the free-market price at $35/oz, but persistent US deficits and speculative demand made the defense unsustainable.

title: Gold Pool collapses; two-tier market
summary: After a run on gold, the London Gold Pool was abandoned in 1968, splitting the official $35 price from a higher free-market price and foreshadowing the end of Bretton Woods.

title: Nixon Shock ends gold convertibility
summary: On August 15, 1971 President Nixon suspended dollar-gold convertibility, ending Bretton Woods and launching the modern free-floating fiat era. Gold began to float and rose sharply.

title: First oil shock and stagflation
summary: The 1973 OPEC oil embargo quadrupled oil prices, igniting stagflation. Gold surged as inflation rose and the dollar weakened in the new floating system.

title: US re-legalizes private gold ownership
summary: Effective December 31, 1974, Americans could again own gold, broadening investment demand just as inflation fears intensified.

title: Second oil shock and geopolitical crises
summary: The Iranian Revolution's oil shock, the Iran hostage crisis, and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan combined with double-digit inflation to drive a parabolic gold rally.

title: Gold peaks near $850
summary: Gold hit an intraday high around $850 in January 1980, the blow-off top of the Great Inflation bull market, before high real rates reversed it.

title: Volcker shock and disinflation
summary: Fed Chair Paul Volcker pushed policy rates toward 20%, producing sharply positive real rates that broke inflation and began a two-decade gold bear market.

title: Plaza Accord weakens the dollar
summary: The 1985 Plaza Accord coordinated a managed dollar decline, giving gold a modest lift within the broader disinflationary bear market.

title: Central bank gold sales and Washington Agreement
summary: Heavy central bank gold selling in the 1990s pushed prices to a ~$250 low; the 1999 Washington Agreement capped sales and helped gold bottom.

title: First gold ETF (GLD) launches
summary: The 2004 launch of the SPDR Gold ETF made gold easily tradable, broadening investment demand during the new secular bull market.

title: Global Financial Crisis and QE1
summary: The 2008 crisis and Lehman's failure triggered zero rates and quantitative easing. Gold first sold off in the liquidation, then rallied strongly as a crisis and reflation hedge.

title: Gold peaks near $1900
summary: The US credit downgrade and eurozone debt crisis drove gold to a 2011 record near $1900 amid open-ended QE expectations.

title: Taper tantrum gold crash
summary: As the Fed signaled tapering QE, real rates rose and gold fell sharply in 2013 despite no inflation spike, illustrating gold's sensitivity to real rates.

title: COVID-19 crash, QE, and record high
summary: The pandemic crash brought enormous monetary and fiscal stimulus; after a brief liquidation dip, gold rose to a record near $2075 in August 2020.

title: 2022 inflation surge and aggressive Fed hikes
summary: With inflation at 40-year highs, the Fed hiked rapidly. Gold was roughly flat for the year despite high inflation, a partial counterexample to the simple inflation-hedge story.

title: Russia sanctions and reserve freeze
summary: After Russia invaded Ukraine, the West froze ~$300bn of Russian FX reserves. This reframed gold as a sanction-proof reserve asset and accelerated central bank buying and de-dollarization.

title: Record central bank gold buying
summary: Central banks, led by China and emerging markets, bought record amounts of gold in 2022-2023, providing structural demand and pushing prices toward new records.

title: 2024-2026 records and reserve shift
summary: Sustained official-sector demand and de-dollarization pushed gold to successive records in 2024-2026 even alongside positive real rates, highlighting a demand-driven valuation regime (illustrative).
